conflicts/reconquista/religionRoleNote: The word 'Reconquista' is a modern label, popularised in the nineteenth century, for nearly eight centuries of intermittent warfare in which Christian kingdoms expanded southwards at the expense of al-Andalus. For long periods the struggle was about land, tribute (the parias paid by the taifa kingdoms) and dynastic rivalry, with frequent alliances across religious lines: the Cid served the Muslim ruler of Zaragoza, and Christian kings fought each other as often as they fought Muslims. Religion became increasingly central from the late eleventh century, when popes granted crusading indulgences for Iberian war (explicitly equated with the Jerusalem crusade by Calixtus II in 1123), the military orders were founded, and the Almoravids and Almohads brought a rigorous ideology of jihad from North Africa. Joseph O'Callaghan stresses the crusading character of the central medieval centuries; other historians warn against reading a continuous religious crusade back into the whole period. 'Major' reflects this variation over time.

conflicts/reconquista/summary: After the Umayyad conquest of the Visigothic kingdom in 711, small Christian realms in the northern mountains gradually expanded southwards over almost eight centuries. Periods of coexistence and trade alternated with raids, conquests and religiously charged war. From the late eleventh century the papacy treated Iberian warfare as crusade, and Muslim dynasties from Morocco answered with jihad. The decisive battle of Las Navas de Tolosa (1212) opened the south; Granada, the last Muslim state, surrendered on 2 January 1492, followed within weeks by the expulsion of Spain's Jews and within a decade by the forced conversion of its Muslims.
conflicts/reconquista/story:
In 711 an Arab and Berber army crossed from North Africa, defeated the Visigothic king Roderic and within a few years controlled most of the peninsula. Tradition dates the beginning of Christian resistance to the victory of Pelagius (Pelayo) at Covadonga in the Asturian mountains, around 718 or 722; the earliest accounts, from the late ninth century, already describe it as a miracle of the Virgin. The small kingdom of Asturias, later León, claimed to be the heir of Visigothic Christian Spain, and its chroniclers spoke of restoring the lost kingdom. The supposed discovery of the tomb of the apostle James at Compostela in the ninth century gave the north a powerful shrine, and the legend of Santiago appearing on a white horse at Clavijo made him 'Matamoros', the Moor-slayer.

For three centuries al-Andalus was the stronger power. Under the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (from 929) it was one of the richest states in Europe, and Christians and Jews lived under it as protected but subordinate dhimmis; some Christians in Córdoba sought martyrdom in the 850s. The regent al-Mansur (Almanzor) led some fifty raids into the Christian north, sacking Barcelona in 985 and Santiago de Compostela in 997 and carrying off captives. After the caliphate collapsed in 1031 into rival taifa kingdoms, the Christian rulers extracted tribute (parias) and began to take territory. Alfonso VI of León–Castile captured Toledo, the old Visigothic capital, in 1085.

The fall of Toledo brought the Almoravids, a Berber reform movement from Morocco, into Spain; under Yusuf ibn Tashfin they defeated Alfonso at Sagrajas (al-Zallaqa) in 1086 and absorbed the taifas. Meanwhile the papacy increasingly sponsored Iberian war: an expedition to Barbastro in 1064, which ended in a massacre and enslavement, attracted French knights; Urban II urged Catalans to restore Tarragona rather than go east; and in 1123 the First Lateran Council and Calixtus II granted the same remission of sins to those fighting in Spain as to those going to Jerusalem. Rodrigo Díaz, El Cid, took Valencia in 1094, having previously served the Muslim ruler of Zaragoza. Alfonso I of Aragon took Zaragoza in 1118, and in 1147 Afonso Henriques of Portugal, helped by English, Flemish and German crusaders sailing to the Second Crusade, captured Lisbon after a four-month siege, followed by a sack in which the Mozarab bishop of the city was killed.

The Almohads, a more rigorous movement which ended the toleration of Christians and Jews in their lands (the young Maimonides' family left Córdoba), crossed into Spain in the 1140s–1170s and crushed Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos in 1195. Military orders on the model of the Templars were founded to hold the frontier: Calatrava (1158), Santiago (1170), Alcántara and Avis. Pope Innocent III proclaimed a crusade, and on 16 July 1212 the combined armies of Castile, Aragon and Navarre, with some foreign crusaders, routed the Almohad caliph Muhammad al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa. The great conquests followed: James I of Aragon took Majorca (1229) and Valencia (1238), and Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba (1236), Jaén (1246) and Seville (1248), where most of the Muslim population left or was expelled. Mudéjares, Muslims living under Christian rule, remained in large numbers in Valencia and Aragon.

Only the Nasrid emirate of Granada survived, often as a tributary of Castile, for two and a half centuries. The Marinids of Morocco intervened until their defeat with the Granadans at the Río Salado in 1340. Under Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile, whose marriage united the two crowns, the Granada War began in 1482 after a Nasrid raid on Zahara. Exploiting a civil war between the emir Abu al-Hasan and his son Muhammad XII (Boabdil), Castilian armies with artillery took town after town; when Málaga resisted in 1487 almost its entire surviving population was enslaved. Papal crusading bulls and the cruzada tax funded the war. Granada surrendered by treaty, and on 2 January 1492 the monarchs entered the Alhambra.

The capitulation guaranteed Muslims their religion, law and property. These promises were soon broken. The Alhambra Decree of 31 March 1492 ordered the Jews of Spain to convert or leave; tens of thousands went into exile. Archbishop Hernando de Talavera of Granada favoured slow persuasion, but Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros imposed mass baptisms from 1499, provoking the Alpujarras revolt (1499–1501), after which Muslims of Castile were ordered to convert or leave in 1502, and those of Aragon in 1526. The converted Moriscos remained suspect, rose again in 1568–1571, and were expelled in 1609–1614. In 1492 also, Columbus sailed under the patronage of the same monarchs, and many habits of the Iberian frontier passed to the conquest of the Americas.
conflicts/reconquista/nameOfGod: Christian kings presented themselves as restorers of a Christian Spain lost through sin, and from the ninth century invoked Saint James 'Matamoros' as the heavenly warrior of the army; 'Santiago!' became the Castilian battle cry. From the 1060s popes offered remission of sins for Iberian campaigns, Calixtus II equated them with the Jerusalem crusade in 1123, and Innocent III proclaimed the crusade of 1212. Military orders of knight-brothers took monastic vows to fight the Muslims. Crusade bulls and the papal cruzada tax financed the Granada War, and the cross was raised on the Alhambra in 1492. On the Muslim side, the Almoravids and Almohads framed their intervention as jihad to defend Islam and purify al-Andalus, and al-Mansur's raids were celebrated as holy war.
conflicts/reconquista/religiousCauses/0: A northern Christian ideology, visible from the ninth-century Asturian chronicles, of restoring the Visigothic Christian kingdom lost in 711.
conflicts/reconquista/religiousCauses/1: Papal extension of crusading indulgences to Iberia from the late eleventh century and the founding of military orders.
conflicts/reconquista/religiousCauses/2: The cult of Saint James at Compostela and the image of Santiago Matamoros as patron of the war.
conflicts/reconquista/religiousCauses/3: Almoravid and Almohad ideologies of jihad and religious reform, which hardened the frontier and ended earlier forms of coexistence.
conflicts/reconquista/religiousCauses/4: In the fifteenth century, Isabella and Ferdinand's programme of religious unity, linked to the Inquisition (1478) and expulsion of the Jews.
conflicts/reconquista/otherCauses/0: Competition for land, pasture, towns and settlers as the northern kingdoms grew.
conflicts/reconquista/otherCauses/1: Tribute (parias) and plunder from the wealthy taifa kingdoms after 1031.
conflicts/reconquista/otherCauses/2: Rivalries among the Christian kingdoms themselves and among the Muslim taifas, which produced cross-religious alliances.
conflicts/reconquista/otherCauses/3: The political fragmentation of al-Andalus after the fall of the Córdoba caliphate.
conflicts/reconquista/otherCauses/4: The ambition of the noble and military-order elites for lordships and of the crowns for royal power and revenue.
conflicts/reconquista/triggers/0: The Umayyad conquest of 711 and the resistance at Covadonga (c. 718/722).
conflicts/reconquista/triggers/1: The collapse of the caliphate of Córdoba in 1031 and Alfonso VI's capture of Toledo in 1085, which drew in the Almoravids.
conflicts/reconquista/triggers/2: The disaster at Alarcos in 1195, which led to the crusade of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
conflicts/reconquista/triggers/3: The Nasrid capture of Zahara in December 1481, which opened the Granada War.

conflicts/reconquista/timeline/9/text: Afonso Henriques and northern crusaders capture Lisbon.

conflicts/reconquista/timeline/12/text: Ferdinand III captures Seville after Córdoba (1236).

conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/1/focus: Led dozens of raids into the Christian north, sacking Barcelona and Santiago de Compostela.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/1/outcom: Died after a campaign in 1002; his dynasty's fall began the collapse of the caliphate.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/2/name: Alfonso VI of León and Castile
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/2/role: King and self-styled 'emperor of all Spain'
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/2/focus: Collected tribute from the taifas and captured Toledo in 1085.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/2/outcom: Defeated by the Almoravids at Sagrajas in 1086 and at Uclés in 1108, where his only son died.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/3/name: Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar, El Cid
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/3/role: Castilian nobleman and soldier of fortune
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/3/focus: Served both Christian and Muslim rulers before conquering and ruling Valencia from 1094.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/3/outcom: Became Spain's national hero through the Cantar de mio Cid; Valencia was abandoned in 1102.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/4/focus: Crossed to Spain at the taifas' request, won at Sagrajas and annexed al-Andalus.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/4/outcom: Founded Marrakesh and united Morocco and al-Andalus.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/5/focus: Defeated at Alarcos in 1195, he led the victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/5/outcom: His victory broke Almohad power in Spain.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/6/outcom: Canonised in 1671; buried in Seville cathedral with epitaphs in Latin, Castilian, Arabic and Hebrew.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/7/name: Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/7/focus: Waged the Granada War of 1482–1492 with papal crusade funding.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/7/outcom: Took Granada, expelled the Jews, sponsored Columbus and later required Muslims to convert or leave.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/8/focus: Fought his father and uncle for the throne and surrendered Granada by treaty.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/8/outcom: Went into exile in the Alpujarras and then Morocco.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/9/role: Hieronymite friar, Isabella's confessor and first archbishop of Granada
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/9/focus: Sought to convert Granada's Muslims by preaching, charity and Arabic catechesis.
conflicts/reconquista/keyPeople/9/outcom: Sidelined by Cisneros' coercive policy; investigated by the Inquisition shortly before his death.
conflicts/reconquista/casualties/note: No meaningful estimate exists for nearly eight centuries of intermittent warfare, raiding and enslavement. Chronicle figures for battles such as Sagrajas, Alarcos or Las Navas de Tolosa are greatly exaggerated on both sides. Enslavement was a major form of harm: al-Mansur's raids carried off thousands of Christians, and the population of Málaga, perhaps around 11,000–15,000 people, was enslaved in 1487, though even this figure is approximate. The Jewish exiles of 1492 are variously estimated by historians at roughly 40,000 to over 100,000.
conflicts/reconquista/effects/0: The Muslim political presence in Iberia ended, and Castile, Aragon and Portugal became dominant Christian monarchies.
conflicts/reconquista/effects/1: Large Muslim populations were displaced, enslaved or reduced to subject Mudéjar status, and later forcibly converted (1499–1526) and expelled as Moriscos (1609–1614).
conflicts/reconquista/effects/2: The Jews of Spain were expelled in 1492 and those of Portugal forced to convert in 1497.
conflicts/reconquista/effects/3: A militarised frontier society, with military orders, municipal militias and the ideal of the warrior-settler, shaped Iberian culture and was carried to the Americas.
conflicts/reconquista/effects/4: Toledo and other conquered cities became centres where Arabic science and philosophy were translated into Latin.
conflicts/reconquista/effectsOnChurch/0: The crusading indulgence was extended to Iberia, and military orders such as Calatrava and Santiago became powerful religious corporations.
conflicts/reconquista/effectsOnChurch/1: The cult of Santiago and the pilgrimage to Compostela grew into one of Christendom's major devotions.
conflicts/reconquista/effectsOnChurch/2: Toledo translations, including the Latin Qur'an commissioned by Peter the Venerable (1143), shaped Western Christian knowledge of Islam.
conflicts/reconquista/effectsOnChurch/3: The quest for religious unity under the Catholic Monarchs produced the Spanish Inquisition (1478), concerns about 'purity of blood' and suspicion of converts.
conflicts/reconquista/effectsOnChurch/4: The Mozarabic rite and community largely disappeared as Roman liturgy and northern clergy replaced older Iberian Christian traditions.
conflicts/reconquista/legacy: The Reconquista became a founding myth of Spanish and Portuguese national identity, emphasised under the Franco regime and still invoked by some modern nationalist movements. Historians now stress that the period also included long stretches of coexistence, cultural exchange and cross-religious alliance (sometimes idealised as convivencia), as well as violence on all sides. The forced conversions and expulsions that followed 1492 are widely recognised as a tragedy for Spain's Jews and Muslims.
conflicts/reconquista/dissenters/0/text: The abbot of Cluny commissioned a Latin translation of the Qur'an in Spain in 1142–1143 and wrote that he approached Muslims 'not with arms but with words, not with force but with reason, not in hatred but in love', though he did not reject crusading itself.
conflicts/reconquista/dissenters/1/text: The Majorcan lay theologian (c. 1232–1316) devoted his life to learning Arabic and to peaceful disputation with Muslims, urging missions rather than conquest, although in later life he also proposed crusade plans.
conflicts/reconquista/dissenters/2/text: As archbishop of Granada after 1492 Talavera insisted on honouring the surrender treaty and converting Muslims by preaching, schooling and Arabic-language instruction, opposing the forced baptisms imposed by Cisneros.
conflicts/reconquista/dissenters/3/text: The Castilian theologian (c. 1393–1458) argued, after the fall of Constantinople, that Christians should seek conferences and dialogue with Muslims rather than war, and prepared a new trilingual Qur'an translation.

conflicts/reconquista/campaigns/1/text: The crusade army assembled at Toledo, retook Calatrava (after which many foreign crusaders went home), crossed the Sierra Morena, routed the Almohads on 16 July and then sacked Baeza and Úbeda.
conflicts/reconquista/campaigns/2/people: Ferdinand and Isabella's Castilian and Aragonese armies
conflicts/reconquista/campaigns/2/text: Beginning with the seizure of Alhama, Castilian armies with artillery reduced the Nasrid emirate piece by piece, besieging Málaga and Baza, and from the camp-city of Santa Fe forced Granada's surrender.
